content:
Quick answer: Managing arthritis at work involves practical adjustments and communication. This includes using ergonomic equipment like adjustable chairs and split keyboards, taking regular breaks to move, and having a plan for flare-ups. Under the Equality Act 2010, employers must make reasonable adjustments if arthritis substantially affects daily activities. Discussing needs with your employer, focusing on solutions, and suggesting specific adjustments is key.

Arthritis at Work: You Are Not Alone

Over 8.5 million working-age adults in the UK live with arthritis. Managing symptoms while maintaining productivity is one of the biggest challenges — but with the right strategies, it is entirely possible.

Know Your Rights

Under the Equality Act 2010, arthritis can qualify as a disability if it has a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities. This means:

  • Your employer must make reasonable adjustments
  • You are protected from discrimination
  • You can request flexible working arrangements
  • Access to Work grants may fund workplace adaptations

Practical Workplace Adjustments

Desk Setup

- Ergonomic chair with lumbar support and adjustable height - Sit-stand desk — alternating positions reduces stiffness - Split keyboard and vertical mouse to reduce hand strain - Monitor at eye level to prevent neck stiffness

Movement Strategies

- Set a timer to move every 30 minutes - Take micro-breaks: gentle wrist circles, shoulder rolls - Use the stairs (if manageable) for gentle exercise - Walk to a colleague's desk instead of emailing

Managing Flare-Ups

- Keep medication at work (with manager's awareness) - Have a "flare-up plan" agreed with your manager - Use heat packs or cooling wraps discreetly - Know your trigger patterns (stress, cold, prolonged sitting)

Talking to Your Employer

Many people fear disclosing their condition. Here is a structured approach:

  1. Choose the right time — a private, scheduled meeting
  2. Focus on solutions — "I work best when I can..." rather than limitations
  3. Bring evidence — an occupational health report adds weight
  4. Suggest specific adjustments — be practical and clear
  5. Follow up in writing — document what was agreed

Useful Resources

  • Access to Work (gov.uk) — grants up to £66,000 for workplace adjustments
  • Versus Arthritis employer toolkit
  • ACAS guidance on disability and reasonable adjustments
  • Fit for Work (NHS service) — free occupational health advice

When to Consider Reduced Hours

If full-time work is no longer sustainable:

  • Discuss phased return or reduced hours with your GP
  • Explore PIP (Personal Independence Payment) eligibility
  • Consider whether your role could be adapted rather than reduced

Written by Emma Richards, Occupational Therapist, NHS England

Practical next steps for Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips

If you came here about Managing Arthritis at Work: Practical Tips, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your local integrated care board about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Work, rights and practical adjustments

Under the Equality Act 2010, employers in Great Britain should consider reasonable adjustments when arthritis has a substantial long-term effect. That can mean flexible hours, more breaks, seating, parking closer to the entrance, or software that reduces typing strain. Acas and Citizens Advice both publish plain-English guides you can take into a meeting.

Benefits conversations

Personal Independence Payment (PIP) looks at how your condition affects daily living and mobility, not the diagnosis name alone. Keep a short diary of bad days, help you need with dressing or cooking, and walking limits. Welfare rights advisers at local councils or charities can check forms before you submit them.

Finding people who understand

Local arthritis groups, hospital patient panels and moderated online communities can reduce isolation. Ask your rheumatology nurse, library, or council adult social care pages for current lists. Choose spaces that feel practical and kind; leave any that push unproven cures or shame medication use.

Quick questions about Managing Arthritis Work Practical

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep learning with us

Explore related guides on Living With Arthritis UK — try the guides hub, diet hub, exercise hub, or site search to filter by topic and length. If benefits or work questions are on your mind, start at the Benefits & PIP hub.

Keep expectations kind while you work on managing arthritis at work: practical tips. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.
